text: You get a sorted array of distinct integers and a target. If the target is in the array, return its index. If it's not, return the index where it would go to keep the array sorted. It has to run in log n time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I don't actually insert anything. I just return the index where it would land. Is that right?
And if the target is bigger than every element, I return n — one past the last index?
Yes. That's a valid answer here.
Good, that's the part I wanted to pin down. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fourth elements, all distinct, sorted ascending.

Here's the observation I want to lead with. The problem sounds like two jobs — find it, and place it — but I think it's one job. Think about gaps instead of cells: an array of n items has n plus one gaps, numbered zero through n. Now ask one question: what is the first index whose value is at least the target? If the target is in the array, that index is the target's index. If it isn't, that's exactly the gap it belongs in. Same number, two readings. So I never need to check for equality at all.

Let me run through the example, with one, three, five, six. For target five, the first value at least five is at index two, and that's where five lives. For target two, it's index one, and two does belong between one and three. For target seven, nothing is at least seven, so the answer runs off the end to four, which is n. All three match the expected output.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would scan from the front until I hit a value at least the target, and return that index. It's simple and correct, but it's linear and ignores the sorted order. This problem reminds me of lower bound from the C++ standard library — a binary search for the first index with value at least the target. So I'll hand-write lower bound as a half-open binary search. The nice part is what I don't write: no early return on equality, no separate not-found path.

Here's the plan. One: keep a half-open range, left to right, starting at zero and n — everything before left is too small, everything from right on is big enough. Two: while the range isn't empty, check the midpoint; if its value is at least the target, set right to mid, otherwise set left to mid plus one. Three: return left. One thing worth flagging — right starts at n, not n minus one. The answer can legally be n, when the target beats every element. If right started at n minus one, left could never climb past it, and every bigger-than-everything input would silently return the wrong number. So the half-open range is what makes n reachable. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The range starts at zero and the array size. Inside the loop I take an overflow-safe midpoint; if its value is at least the target I pull right down to mid, otherwise I push left past it. When the loop ends I just return left. One thing worth flagging — there is no guard before that return, and adding one would be a bug. Coming from the plain search version, my instinct would be to write: if left equals n, return negative one. Here n is a correct answer, not an error. So the guard I'd normally want is exactly the guard I must not write.

Let's dry-run the code with one, three, five, six and target two, the missing case. I expect one. The row that matters is the last: the range is just index zero, and one is smaller than two, so index zero is out and left steps to one. Now left and right are both one, the range is empty, and I return one. Dropping two into index one gives one, two, three, five, six, still sorted. That matches. Corner cases: target five, a hit, returns two. Target seven, bigger than all, walks off the end to four. Target zero, smaller than all, collapses right to zero. A single one with target two returns one.

The time complexity is log n: the range at least halves every round, so about fourteen rounds for ten to the fourth items, and every input pays them all — there's no early exit, by design. The space complexity is constant, three ints and a loop. It always ends: with left below right, mid sits inside the range, so right equals mid and left equals mid plus one both shrink it every round. Oh, one more thing — this function is a building block. Flip the test from at-least to strictly-greater and you get upper bound; subtract the two and you get how many times a value occurs. And the n log n longest increasing subsequence algorithm calls this in a loop, where landing on the length means extend — so n as a real answer shows up again there.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You collapsed find it and place it into one question about gaps before writing any code, which is why your solution has a single return. You explained why right must start at n using the input that would break it. And you named the guard you deliberately did not write, which is the exact spot people carry a habit over from the plain search version. Good work.
